We’ve had OLED touchscreens on Windows PCs since at least 2016 and Lenovo’s Yoga 14, and while the display tech is magnificent it does mean you end up with fingermarks all over your screen, especially if you’re using it after lunch.

Then there's the debate about what touchscreen laptops are actually for. In 2-in-1 designs you can bend the screen back and whip out a stylus for some sketching, but in a traditional laptop you’re more likely to use it for zooming and scrolling. Apple’s announcement event for the laptop showed someone using the touchscreen to play piano keys directly on its screen, and while this somehow seems unlikely, as surely your hands will be in entirely the wrong position, it can also be used to click and drag files, audio tracks, and to do a little precision brushwork with your fingertip if you need to. Happily, it’s optional, and the MacBook trackpad is as good as ever. The touchscreen supports most trackpad gestures, if you’re the sort to let their fingers dance, and as ever you can pay extra for the Nanotexture coating that cuts reflections.

Recent findings suggest that elsewhere, you get the usual MacBook Pro build. They’re really well made, and this one’s no exception. The switch to OLED has allowed for a millimetre to be shaved off the laptop’s thickness, and a few hundred grams to be shed from its weight. The weight reduction is the more noticeable of the two, making Apple’s largest laptop a touch more portable. By far the most vital thing, however, is that the Apple logo on the MacBook’s lid once again lights up when the laptop is in use, and it’s the right way up.

• Thunderbolt 5• Excellent colour reproduction.

In a recent development, there are three Thunderbolt 5 ports on the MacBook Pro 16, all of which are compatible with USB4 peripherals, and as there's a full-size HDMI 2.1 port and a MagSafe 3 for charging, you won’t have to bog them down connecting to monitors and chargers. This opens them up for use with external SSDs, and given the extra cost of upgrading the storage in a modern Mac when you order, one of those will probably be on your shopping list.

Recent findings suggest that the screen is the substantial upcoming feature for this 2026 release of the MacBook Pro 16, and this new OLED is an absolute beauty. It’s a ‘tandem’ OLED, which stacks two light-emitting layers on top of one another for a brightness boost, and it shows: Apple promises up to 2,000 nits of brightness if you feed it HDR content, a figure that rivals even its immensely bright Studio Display XDR. Colour is excellent too though you’ll need to manually activate the PROLED XDR P3 + AdobeRGB colour profile in the Settings app to get the most out of it. Do this, and you can expect 93% of Adobe RGB and 94% of DCI-P3 alongside 100% of sRGB.

Apple has also fiddled with the MacBook Pro’s hinge for a better touchscreen experience. Push too hard and you can find a laptop’s screen leaning away from you, but the hinge on the PROLED is noticeably stiffer than that on a non-touch MacBook. It’s also incredibly smooth, almost like there's some sort of hydraulic aspect to it, as it moves up and down.

On the front you’ll find Apple’s usual keyboard, which is pretty good, and a Force Touch trackpad that can take a bit of getting used to, especially if you’re used to holding the pad in to drag files about. This can trigger a deeper click that brings up file information, which is less useful than you might think, but it doesn’t take long to get the hang of, and you can change what it does in the settings.

Industry observers note that we test every one of our laptops using the same benchmarking software suite to give you a thorough overview of its suitability for creatives of all disciplines and levels. This includes:.

• Geekbench: Tests the CPU for single-core and multi-core power, and the GPU for the system's potential for gaming, image processing, or video editing. Geekbench AI tests the CPU and GPU on a variety of AI-powered and AI-boosted tasks.• Cinebench: Tests the CPU and GPU's ability to run Cinema 4D and Redshift.• UL Procyon: Uses UL Solutions' Procyon software suite to test the system's ability for AI image generation in Stable Diffusion, its Microsoft Office performance and its battery life in a looping video test.• Topaz Video AI: We use Topaz Video AI to test the system's ability to upscale video and convert video to slow-motion.• PugetBench for Creators: We use the PugetBench for Creators benchmarking suite to test the system's ability to run several key tasks in Photoshop and Adobe Premiere Pro, as well as its performance when encoding/transcoding video.• ON1 Resize AI: Tests the system's ability to resize 5 photos to 200% in a batch process. We take the total time taken to resize the images and divide by 5.

• Very fast CPU• GPU can't beat descrete chips.

The PROLED MacBook is a premium product, and so comes with a choice of premium processors (and a premium price, but more on that later). It can be fitted with an M5 Pro, which is what we’ve got here, or an M5 Max that piles on the processing cores. There's no option for anything else, so you won’t be picking one up with a vanilla M5 in it. The M5 Pro and Max both use Apple’s Fusion Architecture to weld CPU dies together into one mega-chip, and the core counts make it look very much like the Pro is two normal M5s stuck together, with two cores disabled. It’s split into six Super cores and 12 Performance cores - the old Efficient cores are missing from this generation - and it can turbo up to 4.6 GHz.

Sources indicate that apple’s claim that the M5 offers the fastest single-core performance out there remains unbeaten in our tests. In the Geekbench 6 single-core test, the M5 Pro comes within a hair’s breadth of the M5 Max in a Mac Studio, a remarkable feat for a laptop. The Studio pulls ahead a bit in the multi-core test due to having more cores, but the Pro is right up there, actually beating the M5 Max from when we tested it in a MacBook Pro and leaving the M4 Pro behind.

Industry observers note that the fastest non-Apple single-core result in our tests, the Asus Zenbook A16 powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Elite, now rests in tenth place in the Geekbench charts, and you have to go to 13th place before you find an X86 CPU, which is in a desktop gaming PC. Apple is completely dominant in this arena at the moment, and it’s only when you switch to the GPU test results that the gaming PCs rise to the top and the Apple chips get some real competition.

In real-world applications, the M5 Pro isn’t as fast at doing tasks such as denoising raw files in Adobe Camera Raw as an Nvidia GPU, but it’s way faster than trying to do it using the integrated graphics on most Intel or AMD chips.

The battery life of all the M5 generation MacBooks has been exceptional, but the OLED screen has tipped the 16in Pro over the edge into a machine that can be relied on for two whole days of use. Testing how long it could play a video until exhausted took a lot longer than on most other laptops, with a final figure in excess of 21 hours. Push it really hard and that will come down, of course, but it’s a remarkable achievement nonetheless.

In a recent development, this is the thing that’s going to keep these first touchscreen Macs out of the hands of many creatives. The 16in model we’ve got here starts at £3,399 for one with 24GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, and just climbs and climbs as you add more stuff to it. You want 64GB of RAM and 4TB of storage? You can have it, but it’ll cost you £5,899 and you can go higher than that if you switch to the M5 Max. The touchscreen is a premium feature, and the same laptop with the old display starts from £2,999. The old M5 model no longer seems to be available, probably to make way for an M6, which is already there on the 14in version.

Industry observers note that the fact this laptop even exists means Apple thinks there's a market for it, and if you’re a touchscreen laptop lover it may be the machine you’ve been dreaming of. There's no denying the expense, however, which means you’re really going to have to love it to consider it over other, better-value, choices.

Thinner and lighter than before.

Excellent CPU performance, GPU can't fight Nvidia.

Closer in performance to the MacBook Pro than to the MacBook Neo, the M5 edition of the MacBook Air is the bargain in Apple's range.

The frist generation of Nvidia's RTX Spark hardware looks promising for creatives. This 14-incher from Asus is powerful, well built, beautifully thin and light, and will last all day on a charge.

A mighty gaming laptop with a powerful GPU can make a good buy for a video editor or designer who likes to work on complex documents. This one from HP is slightly more subtly designed than many, and though its battery life is short it can surely speed up your workflows.

In a recent development, ian Evenden has been a journalist for over 20 years, starting in the days of QuarkXpress 4 and Photoshop 5. He now mainly works in Creative Cloud and Google Docs, but can always find a use for a powerful laptop or two. When not sweating over page layout or photo editing, you can find him peering at the stars or growing vegetables.

"All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the new Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.
  • Industry observers note that the beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes.
  • Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the newly introduced Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the new Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.

Industry observers note that the beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes. You can walk up to them, around them, and through them, but also over them.

Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the newly introduced Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium. The Kowloon High Speed Train Station, designed by Andrew Bromberg of Aedas, is meant to be a continuous curve rising over the waiting hall you can ascend to view over to Hong Kong Island.

And now Snøhetta’s just-completed Shanghai Opera House offers you a cantilevered stair with a view back over the river to the city.

Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks.

There’s only one problem: sooner or later, you will hit a barrier, usually makeshift and consisting of moveable fences and lots of yellow and black tape.

Sometimes the restrictions are monetary. Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks and prospects. The Shanghai Opera House is the latest case: to ascend that-stairway-almost-to-heaven you must pay 50 RMB, or about eight bucks.

Sources indicate that that last move has raised the consciousness of the masses to a much higher degree than the inability to climb Mount Ma in various cities. The digisphere is not happy. Apparently, people feel that photographing themselves against an urban view should be a right, even if the institution giving them that opportunity invested (albeit, in this case, mainly through state funds) in making that experience possible.

Nor is this a problem only in China: all over the world, buildings that were designed to be explored in three dimensions are often subject to restrictions. The fluidity of which architects dream drowns in a sea of concerns about safety and security.

In Europe, the restrictions are a bit more akin to the maze airports have put in your way between security and the gates: you can get to the top of MVRDV’s Depot in Rotterdam or Herzog & de Meuron’s Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg for free, but you have to figure out how, and are meant to be tempted to buy at least a drink along the way.

In our experience economy, that seems par for the parcours to me. Space and views are among the most valuable luxuries on offer, so, until the revolution comes, I do not see the big deal.

A both bigger and smaller issue is the barriers themselves. Even those who confront them in Shanghai and don’t mind forking over the yuan find that the kluges stand in the way not only of free access, but also of the views and of the architecture.

You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

That is because the architects never intended the fences to be there in the first place, so they did not design them into the building. They are the most obtrusive part of the many signs, furnishings, and security devices that festoon buildings especially in China, but all over the world as well.

Industry observers note that the architect Theo Deutinger has written a wonderful compendium, Handbook of Tyranny, listing and diagraming many of the devices that control our movements. Many of them we do not notice, but those that are added after construction stick out the most. You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Recent findings suggest that ironically, part of the reason they are so obvious in China and other Asian countries is because until recently there were so many fewer of them. When the Harbin Opera House opened a little over a decade ago you could clamber all over it, and the same was true of the Kowloon train station.

In recent years, local authorities have become concerned about the same issues that have restricted flows in the Western world. That is largely because of heightened accountability: you can’t easily sue if you trip in China, but local authorities can face consequences from government over mishaps in buildings they oversee – and architects there tell me this is increasingly common.

In a recent development, to be clear, beyond the aesthetic concerns these developments are not entirely negative. Accessibility provisions have often been poor in China, but recently ramps and other devices are opening more spaces to those with mobility concerns – including toddlers and older people who might enjoy these urban landscapes the most. Architects design tiered complexity at the risk of eliminating many users, as Steven Holl, for instance, found out in the case of his Hunters Point Library.

The solution should be relatively simple: architects should design both accessibility and risk-avoidance into their vertical landscapes. Ma’s Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and its surrounding park, designed by Mia Lehrer, already do so (pictured left). There is no reason beyond economics and design complexity that people should not be guided and seduced up and over buildings, even if they might have to pay for that privilege.

When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers.

In a recent development, that leaves only a deeper concern, which is that of the difficulty of fulfilling the promise of fluid space. When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers in and out of covered and even conditioned places. Blobitecture or parametricism offered the same prospects, and Wolf Prix has been screaming for an “open architecture of the open eye, the open mind, the open heart” for decades.

Objective reality stands in the way. Buildings are still buildings – both because of the limits of what structures and conditioning systems can do, leading to the hoary problem of where you put a door, or even a toilet, with sufficient headroom in a blob – and because somebody pays for them.

Inside, as Rem Koolhaas once stated, “all conditioned space is conditional” and outside we are finding that the same is true. You have to pay to play, or for right of way.

As is so often the case, the mountable building landscapes that have been constructed with increasing frequency and at larger and larger scales in the last few decades are more promissory notes for a future open society than built utopias. You can go with the flow and climb any building or mountain, but sooner or later economic and regulatory reality will bring you back down to earth.

He was previously a professor at Virginia Tech School of Architecture and Design and president of the School of Architecture at Taliesin. He has written more than a dozen books on architecture, design and art, including Landscrapers: Building with the Land, published in 2002.

If you regularly commuting to a studio or client meetings, a folding bike is a great investment in your health and wellbeing. It'll get you from the train station to your desk much faster than walking, then fold down small enough to tuck under it unobtrusively.

They aren't cheap, though, which is why the current crop of discounts caught my eye. Three of the most desirable compact bikes on the market right now are right now available at a Black Friday discount, with savings of up to £121.

We’re talking a budget-friendly pedal bike, a hand-built British design classic and an e-bike that's taking aim at the premium end of the market.

In a recent development, two names have shaped the folding bike market more than any other. And the ENGWE Zip brings electric power to the small-wheeled format for less than the price of a pedal-only Brompton.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Liene PixCut S1 is expensive, but its excellent prints, clever templates and fuss-free batch production make it a better dedicated sticker printer than Cricut's StickerPix, and running costs are slightly cheaper.
  • Quality prints, with rich colours and sharp detail.
  • Clever 'Phone Back' feature for custom phone decals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Liene PixCut S1 is expensive, but its excellent prints, clever templates and fuss-free batch production make it a better dedicated sticker printer than Cricut's StickerPix, and running costs are slightly cheaper.

Laminates and cuts stickers in one simple process.

Quality prints, with rich colours and sharp detail.

10,000+ templates and 50,000 graphics to use.

Clever 'Phone Back' feature for custom phone decals.

Some app templates are frustrating to edit.

Recent findings suggest that why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Price: $279.99 (Starter Kit), $346.99 (Inspire Kit); £379.99 (Bundle).

Print tech: Four-layer dye-sublimation thermal transfer (D2T2), with a laminate pass.

Resolution: 300 × 300 dpi, 256 shades per colour.

Sticker size: 4 x 7in; printable area 3.9 x 6.7in.

Photo size: 4 x 6in; printable area 3.94 × 5.83in.

Cutting: Single axis, up to 2ips; fine-point carbide blade, 45-degree angle, 1.0mm tip.

Capacity: 36-sheet paper cassette; ribbon cartridge covers 36 sheets of 4 x 7in.

App support: iOS 9.0+ and Android 4.1+.

Dimensions: 281 x 196 x 104.5mm.

In the box: Printer, paper cassette, 18 sheets each of sticker and photo paper, ink cartridge, blade, power adaptor, manual.

Recent findings suggest that the Liene PixCut S1 prints, laminates and cuts stickers in one go, straight from your phone. It costs between $280 and $347 in the US depending on the bundle (around £349 to £380 in the UK), and it only does a relatively narrow range of things. But it does them very well, and I prefer it to Cricut's StickerPix Print + Cut, even though the PixCut S1 costs around £100 more.

According to recent reports, that distinction becomes more important when you start making several sheets. The PixCut S1 is designed to get a job ready, print it, laminate it and cut it, without having to think too much about the process. It's a specialist machine with an approachable app, and that's actually its biggest strength.

It measures 281 x 196 x 104.5mm and weighs 2.9kg, so it sits on my craft table without taking over and is light enough to shift onto a shelf when you're done. You'll need a bit of clear space at each end for the paper to feed through. Setup is quick. The booklet has clear diagrams for removing the packaging and fitting the cartridge, and the paper tray clicks easily onto the back. Then scan the QR code, install the app, verify your email and pair over Bluetooth. It can pair with up to three devices, which is handy if more than one person in the house wants to use it, or if, like me, you tend to spend the day moving from phone to laptop to tablet without ever settling.

My review unit shipped with a US plug adaptor, so if you're buying in the UK, check what's in the box, but assume, as this is a US-based manufacturer, that you will need to pick up a plug adapter (luckily I review the best drawing tablets, so I have a drawer of adapters).

The PixCut S1 uses four-layer thermal dye sublimation: it lays down colour in passes, then seals it with a protective laminate layer. It prints at 300 x 300 dpi with 256 tones per colour, delivering a smooth, continuous finish rather than the dotty look of inkjet.

It has been revealed that there's no liquid ink here. The cartridge holds dye film, so swapping it is clean and quick, and each one lasts about 36 sheets. It prints stickers on 4 x 7 inch sheets (roughly 3.9 x 6.7 in printable) and photos on 4 x 6 inches. That's the limit of what it can make, so think small stickers, labels, tags and prints rather than substantial projects.

Recent findings suggest that printing times vary from about one to two minutes per sticker sheet, depending on the design complexity. It's quite mesmerising to watch the little printer layer yellow, magenta, and cyan dye as it feeds the design in and out of the printing slot. Looking at the app, you can see each layer scrub down in real time, which is a nice touch.

It has been revealed that the paper tray and cartridge each hold about 36 sheets, so you can work through a decent batch without constantly stopping to replenish supplies. You don't have to print a design, export it, move it into another piece of software, and then set up a separate cutting job. Everything happens in one machine, which makes PixCut S1 feel like what it is: a mini-printer that makes stickers and prints, not a craft machine that wants to do more.

I found the workflow dependable and, importantly, repeatable. Once you've got your design sorted, you can send another sheet through without rethinking the process. That's useful if you're making a set of labels for a small business, preparing gift stickers for Christmas or producing several sheets of your own artwork. It isn't a machine for huge commercial runs, but for short batches it makes a lot of sense.

Industry observers note that speaking of the app, it's incredibly easy to use. If you've used a Cricut and Design Space, you'll know that designing and prepping a job can be a project in itself. Liene's app avoids that because it only has to drive one machine, not a whole ecosystem of craft cutters, printers and heat presses. The Canvas section lets you search templates – type 'boats', and you get a selection – or browse categories like Christmas, holidays and decorative stickers. Pick one, edit it, add your own images and text, and you're away.

The modes are Stickers, Labels, Phone Back, Cards and Invites, and Photos. They all follow the same workflow, so learning one means you've learned the lot, which again plays into the streamlined nature of using the PixCut S1.

There are 10,000+ templates and 50,000 graphics to use, which is a lot, but they're easy to categorise and search.

Stickers are the mode I've been using most during this review because they're so fun and useful. Choose a style (Original, Watercolour or Comic Crew), upload a photo, and the app generates six sticker designs from it. Edit them on the canvas, delete some to make a bigger sticker, or add text and shapes. Hit Make It, load the paper the app asks for, and press Cut.

It has been revealed that labels come with many ready-made designs: pantry, living spaces, medicine, business, names, plus office, planner and bath collections. They're all editable, which makes them handy for home organising or a small business.

Sources indicate that phone Back stood out to me, and I created a number of fun decals, including a Christmas-illustrated pattern from my own photos. It's simple: pick your phone and model from the Apple, Samsung, Motorola and Google ranges, then use a template or build your own with photos, text, shapes and lines. The PixCut S1 prints it, coats it and cuts it to fit your exact model. I haven't seen anything quite like this on other machines, and it highlights what a combined printer and cutter can do that separate devices can't. (You could do something similar on Cricut, but you'll need to measure and design the templates yourself.).

Recent findings suggest that the Photos section covers standard prints, AI portraits, ID photos and collages of up to nine images. The ID photo tool is useful, with on-screen guides to help you frame yourself. The poster option is weaker. Some templates add text I couldn't work out how to edit, which is annoying in an app that is otherwise so flexible.

Photo prints are where the PixCut S1 excels. With 300dpi and 256 tones per colour, you get rich colour and sharp detail, far better than I'd expect from a machine this size. As we're getting overloaded with images, I'm reassured that I can create professional-looking prints from my camera roll at the touch of a button. I tried it with some of my digital art too, and the results were excellent, making professional-quality postcards.

One area where it will excel over the holidays (or for birthdays and events) is cards and gift tags. Cards print on sticker paper and are cut into rectangles, so you can peel and stick them onto a card. Tags are better because you can edit each one separately and print a single tag for one person instead of wasting a full sheet.

The other big difference between the Liene and Cricut is the cost of keeping them fed. The PixCut S1 isn't cheap to buy, but the running costs are more reasonable than you might expect for a dedicated sticker printer. My review bundle includes one cartridge, 18 sheets of sticker paper and 18 sheets of photo paper – similar to the PixCut S1 deal on Amazon. A refill pack with two cartridges and 72 sheets is around £39.99 on Amazon, which works out at roughly 55p per sheet.

Remember that each cartridge is rated for around 36 sheets, so you're getting 72 prints from the two cartridges and 72 sheets of paper in a refill bundle. You also can't buy a mixed sticker-and-photo pack, so you'll need to decide which material you'll use most.

According to recent reports, only Liene's paper works, so it's not a completely open system, and you're limited to 4 x 7 in sticker and 4 x 6 in photo sheets, so you don't get the material variety you would with a Cricut. But the cost per sheet is reasonable for a laminated, cut-to-shape sticker, especially when you fill a sheet with several designs rather than making a single small sticker.

Cricut's StickerPix Print + Cut has a similar restriction around its own paper and cartridges, and its $299.99 / £249.99 price makes it cheaper to buy initially, but its refills cost more at $47.99 / £47.99. But the lower entry price doesn't necessarily make it better value if you'll use it regularly. You're still buying dedicated consumables, and you're also buying into Design Space.

According to recent reports, there's another practical difference when you're making multiple copies. When I used the Cricut, I found that finished sheets need to be manually cleared from the cutting area before the next one can start. It's hardly a deal-breaker, but it adds another little intervention to what should be a simple print-and-cut process. The Liene's appeal is that it feels more like feeding a printer than operating a craft machine.

Recent findings suggest that but oddly, the limitations of the PixCut S1 play into its favour. It's a precise, small and relatively fast device made for one thing – printing and cutting stickers. You're not overburdened with options and can focus on making great prints. Within this narrow category, the PixCut S1 excels and offers options Cricut doesn't, like iPhone case decals. You can create your own templates in Cricut Design Space and fiddle around, but the PixCut S1 does it out of the box for every iPhone (and most Androids).

Here's an at-a-glance look at Liene versus Cricut, because the difference is wafer-thin, but for me, the Pixcut S1 just edges it on running costs and its narrow but specialist nature – especially when it comes to everyday uses like quick phone stickers.

Prints, laminates and cuts stickers in one pass from your phone, using a dedicated app with 10,000+ templates and built-in Phone Back decals. Four-layer dye-sublimation at 300dpi gives rich, sharp prints. It's limited to two paper sizes and Liene consumables, with refills around 55p a sheet.

In a recent development, A cheaper way into print-and-cut stickers, but it runs through Cricut's Design Space app and ecosystem. Refills cost more (£47.99 for 72 prints), it's tied to Cricut's own paper and cartridges, and phone decals mean designing your own templates.

Sources indicate that if you only make stickers occasionally, this is a lot of money for a specialist machine. And if you're mainly after ordinary 6 x 4 inch photo prints, there are cheaper ways to get them. But if you regularly make stickers, labels, phone backs, tags and photo prints – and will make good use of the thousands of templates – it's an easy recommendation.

It won't replace a full craft cutter, and it isn't intended to, but as a focused machine for making stickers and art prints, I prefer the Liene PixCut S1 to the Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut. The Cricut is a bit cheaper and has its own appeal, but the Liene is the more straightforward, better-rounded tool. It feels like something you can keep on your desk and actually use promptly, rather than another craft machine that needs a bit of planning every time you want to make something.

  • In a recent development, the more than 1,000 documents, photographs, drawings, letters, and reports that make up the archive were collected and saved for decades by Annemarie Kusserow, one of 11 children from a Jehovah’s Witness family that lived in the town of Bad Lippspringe in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany.

Five years after the Jehovah’s Witnesses sued the German government over ownership of an archive tracing one family’s persecution by the Nazi regime, the files have been returned to the religious organization, reports the Fresh York Times. Jehovah’s Witnesses were targeted by the Nazis specifically for their refusal to salute Hitler, display the swastika flag, or serve in the military; 4,500 were sent to concentration camps, and 1,800 died during the Nazi era.

In a recent development, the more than 1,000 documents, photographs, drawings, letters, and reports that make up the archive were collected and saved for decades by Annemarie Kusserow, one of 11 children from a Jehovah’s Witness family that lived in the town of Bad Lippspringe in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. According to an oral history published by the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Kusserow home was searched by the Gestapo 20 times, and the Kusserow parents, Hilda and Franz, were the first to be arrested, in the mid-1930s. The children eventually ended up in prisons, concentration camps, or training schools. Two brothers, Wilhelm and Wolfgang, were murdered by the Nazis, and another survived the war but died shortly after from tuberculosis contracted at Dachau. Related Articles Hamburg Culture Prize Renamed After Namesake's Nazi Ties Emerge Switzerland's Bührle Foundation Reaches Settlement with Heirs of Jewish Collector Who Owned Prized Manet.

According to recent reports, at the time of her death in 2005, Annemarie Kusserow’s will stated that her family’s archive should go to the Jehovah’s Witnesses. But one of her brothers, Hans Werner Kusserow, had the archive in his possession at the time, and in 2009 he sold it to the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden. This was “especially troubling,” the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ official website notes, given that her brothers lost their lives due to their pacifism.

Recent findings suggest that the parties came to an “amicable agreement” on November 19, which was formalized the following day by the Higher Regional Court of Cologne. The museum and the Jehovah’s Witnesses agreed to keep the details of the settlement private. A Kusserow relative told the New York Times it is “a great relief that at last we will have these precious documents back where Annemarie always wanted them.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that you’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover swiftly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Recent findings suggest that many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Massive disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Recent findings suggest that going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

According to recent reports, working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

It has been revealed that an occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

According to recent reports, diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

In a recent development, the flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Industry observers note that once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

Mike Craddock, CEO and founder of NewGen, has some thoughts. Before founding the social creator agency, he built a successful career as a professional YouTuber and Call of Duty player, so he knows a thing or two about what makes a strong legacy for a game.

"The further potential for UGC and creator-build mini worlds is massive. In fact, these experiences could become more culturally significant than the original game itself. For Rockstar, that means thinking beyond its post-launch marketing. To move with the times, it needs to give creators the freedom and support to build within the GTA universe – and crucially, not try to control every conversation.".

And as Craddock says, "The measure of GTA VI’s success won’t just be from its launch. It’ll be how it affects pop culture in the years to come.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her position in late 2027, the museum unveiled Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that the announcement coincides with Golden’s 20th anniversary in the role, which she assumed in 2006, and comes just one year after the museum reopened in a new, purpose-built building after a seven-year closure. The new $125 million building was designed by architect David Adjaye and provides 82,000 square feet across seven floors, including a 139-seat public lobby, a rooftop terrace, education spaces, a library, and a cafe. It received rave reviews upon its reopening. Related Articles Zohran Mamdani Spends a Birthday to Remember at the Studio Museum in Harlem Time Magazine Publishes its First Art 100 List, Featuring Artists, Museum Leaders, Dealers and More--See Who Made the Cut.

Kathryn C. Chenault, chair of the museum’s board of trustees, mentioned in a statement that the board has formed a search committee to identify Golden’s successor and has retained an international executive search firm to assist. Golden will remain in her post until a replacement is hired.

While Golden’s departure was not entirely expected, it is not unusual for museum directors to exit their positions after a major renovation or expansion. Lisa Phillips unveiled in September 2025 that she would leave her role as director of the Latest Museum after its reopening, and Janne Sirén, director of the Buffalo AKG Art Museum, said in April that he would step down following the museum’s 2023 expansion.

“I know this is the right moment to begin this transition—and as I look ahead to latest projects and opportunities, I also look back with gratitude toward the many people whose achievements have been my bedrock,” Golden noted in a statement. “I think of my teachers, mentors, and professional colleagues; the long line of Directors, Trustees, and donors who established the Studio Museum and made it thrive; half a century’s worth of endlessly dedicated staff members, audiences, and beloved Harlem neighbors; and above all the generations of artists who have enlightened us. Together, they are an expansive community I cherish that will continue to inspire and enable the next leader of the Studio Museum.”.

It has been revealed that before becoming director of the Studio Museum, Golden worked there as a curatorial fellow. She then joined the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1988 as a curatorial assistant and held several curatorial positions there, co-organizing the 1993 Whitney Biennial and organizing the landmark 1994 exhibition “Black Male: Representations of Masculinity in American Art.” In 2000, she returned to the Studio Museum as deputy director for exhibitions and programs under then-director Lowery Stokes Sims. When Sims stepped down in 2005, Golden was named as her successor.

In a recent development, golden has been credited with raising the profile of the Studio Museum through numerous groundbreaking exhibitions, including 2001’s “Freestyle”. Organized with curator Christine Y. Kim, the show featured 28 emerging Black artists whose work the curators described as “post-Black.” Among the artists championed in that show were Mark Bradford, Rashid Johnson, and Julie Mehretu.

In 2023, Golden won the Dorothy and Lillian Gish Prize, which carries a $250,000 award and recognizes a person who has made a significant contribution to the arts.

Speaking to ARTnews in 2020, Golden described what the Studio Museum meant to her and other young Black creatives:.

[At the Studio Museum], they begin their careers and are able to not only get real professional experience but to form a mission and get a vision of real museum work. I say this as someone whose career is the result of those early experiences at the Studio Museum. It cannot be overstated how significant it was for me, as a 19-year-old art history/African-American studies double major from Smith College, to encounter Dr. Mary Schmidt Campbell, art historian and director of the Studio Museum. I can’t tell you what it meant for me, after over a decade as a curator at the Whitney, to become chief curator at the Studio Museum and to work for Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims, a pioneer in the museum field.

Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

📅 09 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance.
  • Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells.
  • Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Sources indicate that some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Industry observers note that beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health problems that go beyond your hairstyle.

Recent findings suggest that furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

In a recent development, creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing.
  • According to recent reports, wondering how to tell the difference?
  • In a recent development, feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

According to recent reports, wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

In a recent development, feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:.

According to recent reports, caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

In a recent development, chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner prepares suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future prepares feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love aims a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

According to recent reports, shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

Sources indicate that if your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design"

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.
  • The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.
  • It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.

The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.

It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.

The writer and founder of design consultancy A Vibe Called Tech originally came up with the idea for the exhibition while researching her monograph on a century of Black design and was confronted with the lack of documentation she could find on the topic.

“It was a really difficult process because it was just impossible to find any literature or any real evidence of the design work,” she told Dezeen.

This led her to investigate whether any museum reveals today were doing a better job chronicling the work of contemporary Black designers.

“I was like: ‘Oh, there hasn’t been anything like that in the UK that I’m aware of,'” explained the curator.

Sources indicate that with The Nue Black Aesthetic, Prempeh and the Design Museum‘s project curator Tiya Dahyabhai hope to remedy this. The duo has brought together more than 100 works that range from tailored suits to football kits, from minimalist lighting and headphones to a sculptural West African instrument and a trophy for a dominoes league.

Presented together, they act as a rallying cry against the idea that Black design can only look one way, Prempeh claims, allowing its textural and conceptual richness to be experienced in person.

“If people stopped thinking of Black design as just bright colours and wax print, that would be incredible,” she joked.

The show opens with a short look back at the last century of Black design, beginning in the 1920s with Ann Lowe – the first African American fashion designer to become a leading couturier.

“It’s not like Black people weren’t making work before, but in terms of people knowing who they were and there being names and there being evidence of how that work filtered out into the mainstream, that was a really good moment to define,” Prempeh explained.

From here, the show zooms past key moments – the Black Aesthetic movement born out of the Civil Rights era, the pop-infused Newly introduced Black Aesthetic of the 1980s, the ascendancy of African craft led by Diébédo Francis Kéré and Stephen Burks in the 2000s.

The timeline culminates in 2023 with Lesley Lokko’s curation for the Venice Architecture Biennale, which explored Africa as a “powerful place from which to examine the complications that will dominate the next century”.

Against this backdrop, The Nue Black Aesthetic sets out to chronicle the three key topics that seem to be occupying designers across the diaspora today – identity, community and systems.

According to recent reports, “I was looking at the shared ideas that existed within Black design, and those were the themes that kept on coming up again and again and again,” Prempeh explained. “It’s not saying that everyone does everything the same way, but it is saying that there are shared concerns.”.

The first section features work that explores themes of identity.

Here, a C-shaped bench made from a single sheet of metal by Nigerian designer Tejumola Adenuga reinterprets Yoruba design principles, while an intricately embroidered cap worn by the Kanuri people is shown next to a school designed for the displaced community by Lagos-based Oshinowo Studio.

Garments from London fashion designers Bianca Saunders and Saul Nash explore ideas of gender and heritage through cloth, and British-Nigerian artist Taiba Akhuetie reframes Black hair styling as a craft through furniture pieces made from carefully sculpted braids of synthetic hair.

In a recent development, next, the exhibition looks at design as a tool for community building. For some, community comes in the form of sport, as seen in designer Mac Collins‘s monumental trophy for the Nottingham dominoes league and a high-fashion version of Foday Dumbuya‘s viral Pan-African away kit for London football club Arsenal.

Recent findings suggest that phoebe Collings-James, on the other hand, explores community through craft practice. The Jamaican British sculptor contributed a series of experimental pots born from their studio Mudbelly, which offers free ceramics classes by and for Black people through an anti-elitist lens.

Similar themes show up in the work of Ethiopian fashion designer Feben Vemmen, embodied in a luscious, chainmail-style gown she co-designed with bead makers in Accra, and furniture maker Andu Masebo, who contributed a modular, communal table recently used by a rotating cast of 16 musicians during a live eight-hour jam session.

The exhibition’s final section brings together works that aim to challenge the status quo. Some of these challengers come from within; among them Ross, who’s brought his distinctive language to brands like Nike, Zara and Beats by Dre while also running the Black British Artist Grant Association to uplift the next generation of talent.

There’s also Rachel Scott, who is currently weaving her politics into her work for Proenza Schouler, where she became the first Black woman to lead an established American high fashion house when she joined as creative director in 2025.

On the other end of the spectrum are more collectable designs that criticise the system from the outside, courtesy of genre-bending artist Brewster, British-Ghanaian architect Giles Tettey Nartey and Nigerian designer Marcus-Bello.

Standout pieces include a giant contemporary balafon – a predecessor to the xylophone – and a series of aluminium furniture that questions why craftsmen in Nigeria are relegated to working with scraps from the Global North, when the raw materials are mined locally.

The exhibition concludes with a piece created especially for the show by Nigerian-American designer Archibong: a sweeping Murano glass chandelier that hopes to capture the show’s central idea around the whole African diaspora being engaged in one conversation but with very different perspectives and backgrounds.

For Prempeh, the show is also a way to counter the “lack of curiosity around Blackness” – not to mention the open prejudice – which she says has crept back into society since the height of the Black Lives Matter movement.

“I want to present all of the beauty and the depth of Black design as a counter narrative,” she said.

According to recent reports, the Nue Black Aesthetic is on show at London’s Design Museum until 8 August 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 has been out for less than a week, and it isn't just players and critics who are losing their minds. I gave it 5/5 in my GTA 6 review, and it holds a 99 Metascore, tying Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated game ever. As more people play and see more of Leonida, other game developers (those who really know what's what) are lining up to say they're a bit rattled.

In a recent development, the most dramatic reaction I've read came from Igor Sarzyński, creative director on Cyberpunk 2. Reported on Shift Delete, he posted on Bluesky on Saturday evening, two days after launch, and started with "GTA VI-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression is real", then called it "probably the single greatest artistic achievement in history" and "a technological and creative miracle".

He joked that Cyberpunk 2 was cancelled and he was off to sweep leaves in his garden.

Sources indicate that as our sister site GamesRadar+ covered, Sarzyński isn't the only CD Projekt Red game dev impressed. Joint CEO Michał Nowakowski called the game a masterpiece and remarked it's "unbelievably hard" to achieve what Rockstar has. Cyberpunk 2 associate game director Paweł Sasko called it a "generational banger". Witcher 4 director Sebastian Kalemba said he'd love to lose a whole weekend to it, although he's busy hunting monsters for now.

@RockstarGames created a masterpiece that I am planning to explore in the coming weeks and months. Massive congratulations to the whole team who worked on the game. It is unbelievably hard to achieve what you just did. Hats off to all of youNovember 19, 2026.

Over at Naughty Dog, Michael Barclay, who has 19 years in the industry and is working on Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, noted GTA 6 looks to him like "a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child".

It has been revealed that push Square picked up on how Barclay was impressed by the lighting specifically, which he explained is mostly dynamic, yet he states it looks as good as, if not better than, most baked lighting. That's a major deal in an open world where the weather and time of day never stop changing.

Tim Soret of Odd Tales (The Last Night) joined the thread, saying he can't work out how Rockstar gets so many draw calls, hair simulations and volumetric lights running at once.

I’ve made video games for 19 years and GTA VI appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child.November 20, 2026.

None of this surprises anyone who's seen how Rockstar builds its world. As I reported earlier, Rockstar's art team designs buildings by imagining who actually lives in them. And then there's the fact that the animators spend months on small details, like how Lucia opens a door with her hip in a natural way when her hands are full.

VP of art Miriam Bellard says they ask whether a place is messy or tidy, and "what is their taste?" The range runs from industrial and scruffy to decadent and dangerous.

Recent findings suggest that so it seems the people who made GTA 6 are as stunned as everyone else by what they've achieved. As GamesRadar+ reported, Rockstar production coordinator Navya Manaswitha reacted to the reviews by saying she's "truly grateful to be a part of this masterpiece".

I've already argued Rockstar has bucked the AI trend in how it made the game, and GTA 6 is proof that human creativity is still the most impressive technology we have. It seems most game devs agree.

Latest Update: Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears.
  • It has been revealed that whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort.
  • Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home. Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up! Why are my ears clogged? Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked: Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage. If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection. Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side. Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too. Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure. Best clogged ear remedies 1. Pop and unclog The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes. 2. Swallow, yawn, or chew The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow. 3. Ear drops Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes. Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful. 4. Warmth and gravity To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily. 5. Hit the steam room Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 6. Take allergy medication Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears. Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort. 7. Rinse away the gunk Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing. When to see your doctor Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention. What not to do when you have clogged ears Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries. Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion. Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation. Takeaway Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies. PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

It has been revealed that whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up!

Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked:.

According to recent reports, the easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes.

In a recent development, the Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow.

Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes.

Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful.

It has been revealed that to loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily.

Industry observers note that steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths.

Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears.

Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort.

Sources indicate that rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing.

Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention.

Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies.

PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

#91469. Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

📅 10 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2121 w)
